fixes.explanation: That's the king's own read on it. He says, "Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) Nehemiah had just handed King Artaxerxes the wine, and he had never been sad in the king's presence. (Nehemiah 2:1) A king can tell when something's off, friend.

Good guess, but the king never says anything about work. He says it could only be "…sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) King Artaxerxes already knows Nehemiah isn't ill, so he goes straight for what's going on inside. Work isn't in that sentence anywhere, friend.

That's it. The king asks, "What is your request?" and the very next line says, "So I prayed to the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 2:4) The king has just asked his question, and Nehemiah still prays before he answers. I'd have blurted something out and then needed a nap.

No night of thinking here, friend. The king asks his question, and Nehemiah "…prayed to the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 2:4) Then he answers the king. It all happens in one conversation, and I think that's a pretty bold way to handle it.

Close, but that's not the word he uses. Nehemiah asks the king to send him "…so that I may rebuild it." (Nehemiah 2:5) He has just said the city "…lies in ruins…" (Nehemiah 2:3) His request is about building it back up, not guarding it.

Yes, he does. The king, with the queen seated beside him, asks, "How long will your journey take, and when will you return?" (Nehemiah 2:6) Right after that, the text says, "So it pleased the king to send me…" (Nehemiah 2:6) I'd call that a good sign, baker.
Workers aren't part of that request. The letters are "…so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah." (Nehemiah 2:7) That's what the letters are for: getting him through to Judah.

That's the one. Nehemiah asks for "…a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest…" (Nehemiah 2:8) Timber is what he's after. When I need chocolate chips I reach for the jar, but this man writes a letter to the keeper of a whole forest!

Close, but not quite. The text says, "…a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest…" (Nehemiah 2:8) Nehemiah wants timber, and Asaph is the one he writes to for it. Storehouses never come up in the request, friend.

The text doesn't give that as the reason, baker. Nehemiah says, "…because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests." (Nehemiah 2:8) He credits God, and a favor owed isn't something he mentions.

That's the word. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official "…were deeply disturbed…" (Nehemiah 2:10) Sanballat and Tobiah are brand new in the story, and they're already upset. They heard that someone had come to help, and it bothered them.

Worship isn't in this verse, baker. Sanballat and Tobiah were upset that someone "…had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites." (Nehemiah 2:10) Somebody shows up to seek good for the Israelites, and these two are deeply disturbed about it. I think that's a strange thing to be upset about.
